route2019.source: PolarRoute + meshiphi run on NOAA/NSIDC CDR ice of 2019-12-01 (dakshin/figures/routes.json)

window2019.target_note: 'Bharati' is scored at the arrival point of dakshin/figures/routes.json (the nearest water a ship can enter); the station's own cell is ashore and closed every day.
window2019.note: sic_qa_off is what an unguarded reader sees; where it is 0.0 and sic_qa_on is not, the CDR land-spillover filter had suppressed that cell and written it as open water.

alternatives2019.ice_source: NOAA/NSIDC Sea Ice Concentration CDR G02202 v6, 25 km

corridors.label: A
corridors.name: Planned
corridors.rationale: The corridor the prototype has always shown, at the configured 80% working ice limit.

corridors.label: B
corridors.name: Conservative
corridors.rationale: Same ship and ice, limit tightened to 55%. Costs 0.05 days and 34 extra legs - and the worst ice actually sampled along the line goes from 74% to 91%, because the router optimises on cell means while this figure comes from 25 km pixels.

corridors.why: no route exists for this vessel on this mesh — Dijkstra could not connect the waypoints
corridors.label: C
corridors.name: Cautious
corridors.rationale: At a 45% limit no route to Bharati exists at all. Not slower — unreachable. Since 80% is an assumption rather than a certificated limit, this is where that assumption stops being survivable.

findings.finding: Solving for fuel instead of traveltime saves at most 1.6% fuel for at most 0.083 extra days at the limits tested (80%, 55%): the paths differ, but the objectives barely diverge.
findings.why: zero_currents is True and PolarRoute's wave-added-resistance function is dead code in 1.1.11, so fuel differs from time only through the ice term of the fuel rate - not enough to give a real trade-off surface.
findings.consequence: Do not present fuel and time as two objectives until a current or wave field makes them diverge materially.

findings.finding: Tightening the ice limit from 60% to 55% raises the worst ice sampled along the route (74% to 91%).
findings.why: The router plans on cellbox means; the published figure is sampled from 25 km pixels. A cell whose mean is under the limit can still contain pixels far above it.
findings.consequence: The 'heaviest ice on the route' number is not a quantity the router ever optimised against, and must not be presented as though it were.

findings.finding: Bharati is reachable at every assumed limit tested from 80% down to 50%, and unreachable at 45%.
findings.why: Dijkstra cannot connect the waypoints once too many cells close.
findings.consequence: Reachability of the destination rests on an assumed threshold with a cliff edge, not on a certificated limit.

alternatives2019.caveat: Steaming time only. PolarRoute's wave-added-resistance function is dead code in this version, so sea state applies no speed or fuel penalty and every duration here is a lower bound.

vessels2019.verdict: PARTIAL. Changing the ship changes the cost of the plan but not, on this day's ice, the corridor itself: both ships follow the same 63-point track (largest point offset 0.3 km, a smoothing artefact; mesh cells are at least 35 km across), while the ETA moves by 1.30 days and fuel by 9%. So the vessel model is load-bearing for ETA and fuel, and NOT yet demonstrated to be load-bearing for the corridor. The corridor does change when the ice constraint changes (alternatives.json, corridors A and B), so the mechanism works - it is this pair of ships on this day that does not separate it.
vessels2019.do_not_claim: Do not say 'different ships get different routes' on this evidence. Say 'the same route costs this ship 1.30 days more and 9% less fuel'.
vessels2019.note: Both configs carry the same assumed 80% ice limit on purpose. No ice class indexes concentration, so giving the two ships different limits would manufacture the result the test exists to check. Only verified beam, service speed and draft differ — see docs/research/VESSEL_SPECIFICATIONS.md.

resolution.question: does a 1/12° ocean model tell the captain something a coarser model would miss?
resolution.method: same forecasts block-averaged to each resolution, repeated back to the native grid, scored on identical cells; truth and persistence unchanged
resolution.caveat: coarsening one model is not running a coarser model — a true test needs e.g. ANHA runs at several resolutions (see F2, the NEMO-native reader)
hindcast_caveats: sensor change: truth is AMSR2 since 2025-01-01, training truth was F17 SSMIS

berg_hindcast.wind: zero — a stated limitation, not an approximation: measured R (assumed 10 m/s wind) has median 0.25, max 1.73 across segments; coupling the harvested ECMWF wind into the drift is open work
caveats: USNIC positions are accurate to only a few km
weekly fixes: errors mix drift-model error with fix-timing error
grounded-or-unknown segments are excluded from the km/day summary but listed in full

split.finding: most corridor giants are grounded (persistence 0 km); a current-advection model without grounding detection drifts anchored bergs, and persistence also wins on the moving sample at weekly fix cadence

v2_grounding.assumption: keel draught 208 m (0.83 x assumed 250 m thickness; USNIC publishes none)

berg_resolution.question: does eddy-resolving current resolution matter for giant-berg drift in this corridor?

caveats: coarsening one model's currents is not running a coarser model
